reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Presbycusis is the progressive, symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss that accompanies ageing and is the commonest cause of hearing loss in older adults
It characteristically begins with the high frequencies, so patients first struggle with consonant sounds and with speech in noisy or crowded settings
A common complaint is that people can hear that someone is speaking but cannot make out the words, reflecting impaired speech discrimination
Tinnitus and difficulty localising sound frequently accompany the hearing loss
Audiometry typically shows a bilateral, symmetrical, high-frequency down-sloping sensorineural pattern
Recruitment (abnormal loudness growth) can make amplified sound uncomfortable and complicate hearing aid fitting
Contributing and aggravating factors include noise exposure, ototoxic drugs, vascular disease and diabetes, which should be addressed
Management is largely rehabilitative with hearing aids, assistive listening devices and auditory training, and cochlear implantation is considered for severe cases with poor aided benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Presbycusis results from cumulative degenerative changes in the auditory system with age. Several subtypes are described: sensory presbycusis from loss of hair cells in the basal (high-frequency) cochlea; neural presbycusis from loss of spiral ganglion neurons, which particularly impairs speech discrimination; strial or metabolic presbycusis from atrophy of the stria vascularis affecting the endocochlear potential across frequencies; and cochlear conductive (mechanical) presbycusis from stiffening of the basilar membrane. Central auditory pathway changes further degrade processing of speech, especially in noise. Genetic predisposition, lifelong noise exposure, vascular and metabolic disease and ototoxins accelerate these changes.
additionalDifferentials: Cerumen impaction or middle ear disease causing conductive loss
Acoustic neuroma or other retrocochlear lesion (especially if asymmetrical)
Metabolic or autoimmune inner ear disease
additionalInvestigations: Pure tone audiometry to confirm the symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural pattern
Speech audiometry to assess discrimination and predict hearing aid benefit
Tympanometry to exclude a middle ear conductive component
Otoscopy to exclude wax impaction and other external or middle ear disease
MRI of the internal auditory meatus if the loss is markedly asymmetrical or there is unilateral tinnitus
redFlags: Marked asymmetry between ears suggesting a retrocochlear or other unilateral lesion
Sudden or rapidly progressive hearing loss requiring urgent evaluation
Unilateral tinnitus, vertigo or facial numbness raising concern for acoustic neuroma
Associated neurological signs that point away from simple age-related loss
reference.prognosis: Presbycusis is irreversible and slowly progressive, but most patients maintain good communication and quality of life with hearing aids and rehabilitation, and cochlear implantation can help those with severe loss and poor aided speech understanding.
pitfalls: Assuming all hearing loss in the elderly is presbycusis and missing wax, effusion or a tumour
Neglecting the impact of poor speech discrimination and recruitment on hearing aid success
Failing to address modifiable contributors such as ongoing noise exposure and ototoxic medication
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Hearing aids as the mainstay, amplifying the high frequencies where loss is greatest
Cochlear implantation for severe loss with poor aided speech discrimination
Aural rehabilitation, assistive listening devices and communication strategies to support speech understanding, especially in noise
Tinnitus management with education and sound therapy where troublesome
Address modifiable contributors such as noise protection, avoidance of ototoxins and control of vascular and metabolic disease to slow progression
Periodic audiological review to monitor progression and optimise amplification
